newsitem.title: EGYPT: Iraq hopes to "clear the air" with U.S. - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Iraq hopes to "clear the air" with U.S. - envoy.

text.p: Iraq's ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva said in remarks published on Wednesday that Iraq hoped to "clear the air" with the United States now that President Bill Clinton was re-elected.

Barzan al-Tikriti also told the London-based Arabic newspaper Al-Hayat that President Saddam Hussein would not sit idly by and see Iraqi people suffer if he lost hope that Gulf War sanctions would be lifted.

"Now that elections are over, and President Bill Clinton is re-elected, we hope he would be more clear and serious in his second term toward Iraq...especially as Iraq is ready to clear the air with America and discuss common interests which could be important to stop declining ties," he said.

The United States under former president George Bush led a multinational coalition that ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait in 1991, and Clinton has persistently followed a policy of isolating Iraq.

"What I can say is President Saddam Hussein, the government and the Iraqi people will not just go on sitting as some imagine, especially when they become sure that there is no hope on the horizon," the ambassador, who is also Saddam's half-brother, was quoted as saying.
United Nations sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait prevent Baghdad from exporting oil.

Washington has played a key role in delaying an oil-for-food deal signed by the United Nations and Baghdad in May allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to raise money to buy urgent needs for the Iraqi population.
"I would say that President Saddam Hussein knows the details of the daily suffering of his people and that's why he will not stand by before the sanctions are lifted," Tikriti said.

"President Saddam Hussein doesn't walk in the same path twice, and therefore if things get complicated, God forbid, nobody will be able to guess which path he will take or from where the next blow will come," he said without elaborating.
